In the film, Lumumba, we see the faces behind the monumental shift in the Congo's history after it is reclaimed from the Belgians, and we see the motives behind those men into whose hands the raped and starving country fell. Lumumba is not a movie for the hyper masses; it demands the attention of its viewers with raw, truthful acting and intricate, packed dialogue. Little of the main plot is shown through action, it relies almost solely on words, but there is a recurring strand that is only action, and it is the stroke of genius that makes the film an enlightening and powerful panorama of the tense political struggle that the Congo's independence gave birth to. This film is real. It is raw inits depiction of those in power, and those on the streets. It is eye-opening in its content. This is an extremely involving series that takes you into the life of a terrorist agent and the undercover world. We follow Michael Ealy as the FBI undercover agent Darwyn who has to infiltrate a terrorist cell lead by aal (Oder Fehr). The series is extremely well written, and has enough plot twists to keep you sitting at the edge of your seat waiting for whatever happens next. Michael Ealy is by all definition one of the best actors I've seen portray an undercover agent. Icey cold on the outside, but still a good person underneath, trying his best to keep his head clear during a very emotional roller-coaster ride that could have had him going insane. Oder Fehr on the other hand comes off a guy who pretty much could fit into any terrorist scenario. Rough and charismatic, but yet able to disappear into the gray mass if so needed. Highly intelligent and extremely cunning. The way these two communicate on screen is nothing short of brilliant. The way the story unfolds, and the level of detail in the writing, makes the whole series extremely interesting, but also very true to life. The level of detail is of such magnitude that you are left with a feeling of unease, not knowing what might happen in the real world. We read about terrorism every day, and here we are, getting a sneak peek into an underground world that most of us know very little about. It's a series that will most definitely have you coming back for more, and sitting at the edge of your seat just waiting for the next episode to come on. It's a sure winner in my book, and I have no problems stating that this series is on my list of all time best.

Though I saw this movie dubbed in English, so I could watch it at home in the States, without French accents, I thought it was an excellent and refreshing movie. It's set in a hotel room (a real pick-me-up that is) and explores the complexities of family relationships, the role of the "gay" within the family, where one is supposed to belong in society, what it's like to be gay-ish, etc. I was surprised that a French television movie had such a positive and accurate portrayal of the gay community. While the fact that the main gay character ends up with "someone" in the end is mildly disappointing, it's life, and that happens sometimes. This is a great movie, whether you're gay or not! A really enjoyable experience

I saw this episode of Masterpiece Theatre and immediately came to IMDb to look it up. I was greeted by a comment from another user, who believed that it was nothing special, a 6 out of 10, and underwhelming. I would feel morally remiss if I didn't disagree. Now, I am an avid fan of Masterpiece Theatre, but oftentimes the stories can be a bit silly on television, for example, "He Knew He Was Right" was absolutely horrendous. "Carrie's War," however, is probably the best I've seen so far. The entire cast does an excellent job, and it held my interest more than any other piece I've seen recently. The character Mr. Evans is of particular interest, and through subtle images of, for example, an untouched birthday cake or a garnet ring, my opinion of him went from bad to truly good. Truly. His ultimate demise, and the story of how everyone around him left him a cold hard man, is what brought out the bittersweet in this story for me. The end is gratifying in every sense but one; that everyone did not get what they deserved, but overall things worked out. I absolutely recommend this to everyone.

I saw this gem of a movie, and immediately came to IMDb to look it up. I was greeted with negative reviews from other critics, who believed that it was nothing but predictable, unoriginal, and 100% underwhelming. I would be morally remiss if I did't disagree. First of all, I am a huge fan of Carrie'sshaw, but sometimes her stories can be a bit silly on television, for example, "I Knew He Loved Me" was absolutely laughable. "Carrie's Wedding," however, is probably the best I've seen so far. The entire cast did an excellent job, and it held my interest more than any other movie I've seen recently. The character Mr. B, was well-developed, and through the use of, for example, an old watch, or a signet ring, my perception of him went from evil to villainous. However, his ultimate demise was not a surprise, as everyone knew that he was a very dangerous man. The movie gives out a bittersweet ending, as the protagonist's success in the end is gratifying in itself, but also shows that everyone did not get what they wanted, but that things worked out. I highly recommend it to everyone.

L'OSSESSA, also known as THE TORMENTED or THE SEXORCIST, or the ridiculously titled THE EERIE MIDNIGHT HORROR SHOW, is a forgotten EXORCIST rip-off which contains one of the best horror moments I've ever seen. The scene is when the crucifix comes alive. This great spooky scene is unforgettable and totally effective (great FXs). It's a shame the rest of the movie doesn't maintain the level of creepiness exemplified during that scene. This is one of the most frustrating movies ever. Imagine the producers deciding to to make an EXORCIST copy but while making it, they actually succeed in creating something truly original (a possessed sculpture of crucified man, which is shocking when you think about it) but then completely forgets their original idea in order to make a boring and uninspired EXORCIST rip-off. Had the film continued with the possessed sculpture concept (with the characters trying to destroy it, etc), this film would have rocked. But once the girl becomes possessed by the spirit of the sculpture, she never tells anyone from where the demon came from. She, and the script, completely forgets the haunted crucifix, which is STUPID!!! If you like so-called "Euro-cult" movies, the first 45 minutes deliver unlike any other Euro-cult movies. But after the scene when the girl has a vision of being crucified and she gets stigmatas, the remaining 45 minutes SUCK. Boring. It goes nowhere fast as it tries to emulate (badly) THE EXORCIST. So, watch the first 45 minutes of L'OSSESSA and enjoy the 1970s fashions, the sleaze and the amazing statue-comes-alive-to-ravish-the-girl scene but after the first 45 minutes, press stop and eject, and might as well go clip your toenails.

Crackerjack is a simple but feelgood movie where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is tempted by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the central setting being the local lawn bowls clubs drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens - and all laughed at the comedy. As would be expected of a movie with Mick Malloy and Judith Lucy there was quite a bit of swearing, but it was not overdone and the audience I sat with certainly enjoyed it! Mick Malloy did a good job as the lazy bloke who joined the bowls club (three times) simply to get parking spaces (one for himself and two for leasing to others at a premium) but who has everything fall down on him when he is required to play or lose his membership. Judith Lucy does a fine job as his local journalist/love-interest and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Frank Wilson, Monica Maughan, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not one of his funniest but he gives a solid performance. The not so subtle swipes at pokies provide a bit of a serious note to this otherwise light comedy. I'm sure that those who enjoyed The Castle and The Dish would also enjoy this movie.

The movie is is is a light and light comedy where the good guys are very good and the bad guys are very bad and the central character is loved by both sides. The combination of the central character being played by Mick Malloy and the setting being at the local lawn bowls club drew an unusually broad crowd ranging from large numbers of teenagers to large numbers of senior citizens, and all groups enjoyed the comedy. As would be expected in a movie with Mick Malloy and friends, there was quite a bit of humour, but it was not overdone and the people I sat with certainly enjoyed it. Mick Malloy gives a great performance as the ultimate good guy who joined the bowls club (three times) simply because the parking spaces (one for himself and two for friends) were at a premium, and who has everything fall down around him when he is about to play or lose a game. Lana Lucy does a fine job as the good guy's wife, and there are fabulous performances from Bill Hunter, Richard Wilson, David P.ton, Lois Ramsey and many others. John Clarke's dour role as the bad guy is not his best work, but he gives a solid performance, and Mick Malloyloy's swipes at him provide a bit of a sharp edge to an otherwise light comedy. I'm sure that those who enjoyed The Castle and The Dish would also enjoy this.

I think he should stick to playing more "Dirty Harry" type roles, but he played them well. There were some negatives this time, though, namely the credibility in parts as there were a couple of scenes that should have been left out, and I would have done better with Eastwood. The series finally started to grow into a very qualitative series. Too bad they had to cancel the series. Because the last episodes of Cleopatra 2525 actually was very good. I will never forget Hel, Sarge and Cleo. Unique characters that only the creators of Xena could have created!

There are moments when you just want to watch a simple movie, with lots of action and cool characters. For those moments, you have Cleopatra 2525. I'm one of those people who loved Charlie's Angels. Sure, it was very superficial and silly. But the thing is, it was so fun! People who can't relax and are too serious will find it boring. It's the same with Cleopatra 2525. It is superficial. It is full of unrealistic characters. And that's why I like it. It's not like any other series. The first season wasn't very good. The character Sarge was irritating and he talked too much. The plot was a little slow, and we didn't get to know the characters very much. But hey, we only had 30 minutes in every episode. In the last 5-6 episodes of Cleopatra 2525, they finally gave the series full 60 minutes of length. And that was when it started to get better. The characters finally started to grow in a more qualitative way. Too bad they had to cancel the series. Because the last episode of Cleopatra 2525, was simply best. I will never forget Max, Sarge and Cleo. The characters that only the creators of this series could have made!

Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man was found wandering around London in a space-suit, if the passenger of a Rolls Royce suddenly transmogrified into a skeleton, if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, you called on 'Department S' to sort things out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the department was headed by a black man - 'Sir Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis Alaba Peters ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers & Partners, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.T.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! Trivia Note: the episode 'A Small War Of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in a major role!

Written by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a science thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve the bizarre mysteries the police couldn't crack. If a plane landed at an airport with no one aboard, or a man was found wandering the streets in a space suit, or if the passenger on a high-speed train was transmogrified into a skeleton, or a train stopped into a crowd that turned out to be dead commuters, it was on 'Department S' to sort it out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jonathan King', a brilliant but eccentric scientist, who used his fertile imagination to crack many of the bizarre cases that had caught the public's fancy. It was not a one-off show, however. Jonathan was assisted by brilliant 'Dr. Sullivan' ( David Suant ) and the equally eccentric 'Dr. Hurst' ( Rosemary Thorne ). Unusually for a 'women's' show, the department was overse run by a man, 'Sir Malcolm Sinclair' ( played by Michael Gon. ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was not surprising. They shared many of the same writers and directors. The colourful titles were designed by Chambers and Chambers, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.B.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His score for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best TV scores of all time. Predictably, the show seems a little dated and cheesy now, but don't let that dissuade you from watching it. Imagine a hybrid between 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! ( Note: the episode 'A Small War of Nerves' does not feature Sir Malcolm as in the series )

Not your everyday Tom and Jerry short for several reasons. First, it has a bit of narration to it, which is unusual for a Tom and Jerry short film. Second, the two are friends, which was a rare and seldom seen dynamic compared to the more adversarial shorts produced. Third, and most importantly, the cartoon is rarely humorous (by design), but the humor here is more subtle, and manages to cough up a bit of laughter in the end. Pat O'Brien had his best role ever as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. From humble beginnings, Rockne entered Notre Dame as a student circa 1910. He is into chemistry but becomes a marvelous football player and hero. Upon graduation, he teaches chemistry at the school but he has got the football fever that tugs at him, this forces him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching the game. In a way, too bad, the school probably lost a great chemistry teacher-certainly far better and nicer than the one I had in high school. (Erasmus Hall in Brooklyn to be exact.) He motivates his students. He will not tolerate academic underachievement. He is a coach for all seasons. O'Brien captures that common kind touch. One of his students, George Gipp, is memorably played in a fine brief supporting performance by Ronald Reagan. The years pass and the achievements run high-but Knute remains the same kind coach who testifies before Congress when football is called into question. Donald Crisp is outstanding as a Notre Dame priest who knew that Rockne was destined to coach football. Albert Basserman is adequate, but his Jewish accent in the portrayal of a priest is awkward at best. Basserman was nominated that year in the supporting category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's tragic death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of many more years of a totally professionally wonderful human-being. The film is great.

Pat Rockne is a very good portrayal of Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. In the film, Rockne enters Notre Dame as a freshman in 1910. He is into football and becomes a marvelous football player and coach. After graduation, he teaches chemistry at the school but he has a constant football fever that tugs at him, this causes him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream as a football coach. In a way, too bad, the school probably lost a great teacher. Rockne is much better and nicer than the teachers I had in high school. (Erasmus Hall in Brooklyn to be exact.) He motivates his players, and will not stand for underachievement. He is a coach for all seasons, and he does't have that common sports mentality. One of his players, George Gipp, becomes a star, in a fine brief role played by Ronald Reagan. The years pass and the achievements mount, but Rockne remains humble and kind. He testifies before Congress when he is 70. Donald Basserman is great as a Notre Dame student who thought that Rockne was a bit and a Jew. Basserman is Jewish, but not Jewish, and his portrayal of a Jew is awkward and funny. Basserman was nominated that year in the supporting category for "The Big Sleep." Rockne's early death, from a heart attack, robbed the world of many more years of a great and wonderful human being. The film is great

Zeppelin is my favorite band, so when I heard that this new DVD was coming out, I was understandably excited. I'll just cut to the chase here, and say that if you're any kind of Zeppelin fan, you must run out and buy this right now. It's absolutely spectacular. It blows 'The Song of Led Zeppelin' completely out of the water. The footage that was never seen before is simply amazing. The footage on here shows the Zep at the peak of their game, which I never really felt the 'Song' DVD did. Jimmy Page is his best ever without a doubt, and he'd make Jimi Hendrix look like a novice. Of course, the video for the epic jam 'White Dog' is a must-see. Hats off to Jimmy Page, and Robert Plant and Led Zeppelin! 11 out of 5

This cheapo remake of the classic Five Star Murder is a hot mess. Humphrey Bogart stars as the manager of a sleazoid radio station that is desperate to boost sagging ratings. The station decides to have a series of radio plays written about a famous murder case that happened a few years ago. So they hire a fake detective (Harry Hayden) to track down the murderess, who was acquitted and has been living quietly under a different name. The plays go on the air the next day, but the murderer hears the plays and runs off exposing her mother and ruining their lives. Bogart is always great. Hayden is good the the phony detective, and Henry Bateman is good as the murderer. Everyone else is just bad. Helen McKeller wins no sympathy (crucial for the plot), Claire Dodd is a dud, Beverly Roberts is pretty but always looks bored, Claire Dodd and Bogart's hot but have no chemistry, Carlyle Johnson is a dud as the radio producer, Virginia Grey is a dud as the murderer's mother, Robert Middlemas overacts as the station owner, and Boris Karloff is is underused. This is a pale imitation of the original which boasted great performances by Edward G. Robinson, Aline MacMahon, Claire Dodd, and Boris Karloff. But it's always worth watching Boagrt

Hey, a fellow IMDb user. I enjoyed this show a lot. The good news is, it didn't try to be more than it is; a cheesy, cheesy sitcom with low expectations. The bad news is the repeated plot points, one-dimensional characters, and trying to appeal to a post college audience. I guess this is what happens when you make shows about people trying to be mature, in a cheesy, immature way. The writing cast, as always, delivers with witty dialogue and hilarious one-liners. The humor is very 90's, taking advantage of the tendencies of the new millennium. This is the only reason in my opinion why this show has a cult following. It's stuck in a time of its own. Oh, yeah. The main character is funny and perky. I's just not hard to believe that a show that deals with Karma biting your ass will become a cult classic. I'm sure it's part of the charm of the show, though.

"Half Empty" is a hilarious musical about the eternal optimist in this case, a self-help book writer who goes to Germany mistakenly thinking he's popular there. Instead of an adoring audience, he finds himself adrift in a world of jaded misanthropes, including the woman who is supposed to be his publicist. His attempts to make friendsin scenes that are largely improvisedlead to one great encounter after another when he is verbally abused by nihilistic musicians, gruff gangsters, etc. In time, he manages to win over his publicistboth her heart and her mind--but his own world view is shaken when his hero, a much more popular self-help writer, turns out to be not quite what he seems. The action is punctuated by several musical numbers. We saw this at the DeadCenter film festival in Oklahoma City and were blown away. This is a really funny, inspired small-scale indie production. You could quibble about a few technical things (like the lighting, which is a bit dark) but the piece is funny and inspired enough that you can't care too much. If Voltaire were writing "Candide" today, the character would be a self-help writer.

"Half Light" is a dark comedy about an American optimist  in this case, a self-help book writer who goes to Germany mistakenly thinking he's popular there. Instead of being greeted by ad and fans, he finds himself in a world of criminals and misanthropes, not the least of whom happens to be his publicist. His attempts to prove himselfin scenes that are largely improvisedlead to one great disaster after another: he's verbally abused by nihilistic students, threatened by gangsters, etc. In time, he manages to win over his publicistboth her heart and her mind--but his own world view is shattered when his hero, a self who is a similarist, turns out to be not quite what he seems. The action is punctuated by several musical numbers. I saw this at the DeadCenter film festival in San Francisco and was blown away. This is a great film for a small-time indie filmmaker. It could be improved by a few technical things (like the lighting, which is a bit dark) but the piece is funny and engaging enough that you don't care too much. If there were a "Candide" movie, the character would be a self-help.

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

A nice entry in the Crime Squad series [#9/10], with a lot of color in black and white, and some splendid Spanish Americana music and dancing. And a rather off-the-wall plot too. A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a hotel room after a lavish dinner party. The Crime Squad is on the case (as well as a private detective to immediately confirm the identity of the crime) and so we are presented with a rather odd set of suspects to identify the killer, for none of them did the deed. Was it the frothing husband of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and wealthy widow Hilary Brent, the young brother and sister duo, the lovely young maid, the rather doctor Mr. Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or the Chief of the New York Police Department? The film is cut well, with Warner Baxter as the lead, as usual, and the team Squad slowly working it all out. Some of the goofs seen on the screen are classic: Upon breaking into the murder scene Ordway says "Right in the middle of the night" and the maid replies "He didn't miss this time"; Favorite duo Ordway and Baxter getting themselves through club soda and beer at the nightclub; The scene of the interrupted dinner party; The scene where the maid is in place of the maid, seemingly from nowhere. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it's all tied off is perhaps not worthy of the series, but leaving it in the air wouldn't have been good either. Well worth a watch if you already like the series, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the series.

All I can say after watching the DVDs of the first season is that I can not believe NBC "green-lighted" this show. It's so different than what's currently in vogue save for Lost. Those who miss the X-Files just may have a worthy successor. Not as mysterious or intense as Lost, I find it to be overall more entertaining. This kind of extended story is hard to make. I mean it could degenerate into childish dribble if most of the elements do not cohere together. But cohere they do and I think the cast is excellent, the writing sharp, the location and props first rate, and the special effects very good for a television budget. Sure it pushes what is plausible, but as it does it never gets so silly as to insult your intelligence. Bottomline is that this is great Sci-Fi drama for the entire family. I doubt it will be a classic with a long run like X-Files, but in the meantime I recommend getting the DVD if you missed it like I did the first time around. This fall my must see shows has just increased by one more series! PS: I just heard it got axed from NBC...Here's hoping Sci-Fi picks it up.

I must say it was a let down. Overall its great to see the way Aparna Sen has handled the issue of schizophrenia, I am not much knowledgeable on this and got whatever it was depicted in A Beautiful Mind, and here too its interesting portrayal. But the thing that caused the let down for me was the artificial dialogues and over use of English. Its true that a new class is being formed/ has been formed in India which talks in English even at home, but I am sure its not as formal as in the movie. Moreover, Waheeda Rehmaan did not seem very comfortable talking everything in English. Charu's dialogue in Bihari tone was seemingly much more realistic and digestible. The second thing, its about the abstract flavor she has tried to give to the movie. I generally like movies with open ending, but here there were many loose ends. Its like cut pieces are joined together to make the movie. Also there seemed no central theme to the movie. Schizophernia for sure was the main line but intermingling sister-sister, mother-daughter, adding doctor-azmi relation, no real use of brother, Bose - Bose's wife relations..... all were not required and made the audience loose track of what actually did she try to depict. On the whole, a watch for people who like off-beat movies, a must avoid for the ones who just see movies as an entertainment tool.

I must say it was a good movie. It was great to see the way Aparna Sen has handled the story. However, I have seen a story like this and got how it was depicted in A Beautiful Mind, and that too in English language. But the thing that caused the most discomfort for me was the dialogue and the overuse of English. Its true that a new class is being formed or has been formed in India which talks in English even at home, but I am sure its not as widespread as the movie suggests. Moreover, Waheeda Rahman's dialogue did not sound very comfortable to me as compared to Charu's dialogue in Bihari which was seemingly much more natural and digestible. The other thing, its about the abstract flavor she has tried to give to the movie. I generally dont like an open ending, but here there was no proper ending. Its like cut scenes were joined together to make the movie. Also there seemed no central theme in the movie. The story of the search for truth was the main line but the use of the abstract scene, the flash scenes, adding doctor-azmi's character, the use of music, the use of inter family relations..... all were not necessary and made the audience lose track of the actually theme she wanted to depict. Overall it is a must watch for those who like off-beat movies and a must avoid for those who want to see a conventional movie.

Travis and Sandy(Ben Johnson and Harry Carey, Jr.)are horse traders coerced into selling their animals to a Mormon group and guiding them across the frontier to a settlement. What they do not expect is to encounter the notorious Clegg murderers, with their wounded leader Uncle Shiloh(Charles Kemper). Ward Bond portrays Elder Wiggs, the main voice for the Mormon group moving the wagon train to the Lord's destination. Along the way, they also encounter "Doctor" A Locksley Hall and his "Hoochey Koochey Wagon" and lend them help. Lovingly directed by Ford who pays close attention to detail with realistic problems any group would encounter during a rugged wagon trail. The film has a wonderful cast made up of character actors with nary a true star in the film which is actually a blessing to see, if just not for a change of pace. Young Johnson and Carey, Jr. come off real well, but this is Bond's film to shine as he has the best lines. Johnson is the one who seems to understand ruffians and brutes like Shiloh and will certainly come in handy when certain conflict might develop as the Clegg boys ride along side them a piece. I'd have to say this is one of his best and most least appreciated westerns and seems to flow very well.

Travis Ford and Harry Carey, Jr. play the roles of two horse traders coerced into selling their animals to a wagon train and guiding them across the frontier to the west. What they do not expect is to encounter the notorious Clegg's gang, led by the ruthless Uncle Tom Clegg(Charles Kemper). Ward Bond portrays the guide who is the main voice for the entire group from the wagon train to the Clegg gang. Along the way, they also encounter "Doctor" Adams (Jon Hall) and "Hoochey" Smith ( (John Wayne) who lend them help. Lovingly directed by Ford who pays close attention to the survival instincts of any of those out on the rugged western trail. The film has a wonderful cast made up of character actors with nary a true star in sight. It is actually a joy to watch, but just not everyone's cup of tea. Larry Donner (Billy Crystal) has a crazy life: His wife (Kate Mulgrew) stole his book and left him, he has a new budding romance with a girl named Beth (Kim Greist), he doesn't know how to start his book, and his students of his screen writing class are stranger than most. Larry Crowne (Billy Crystal) has a crazy life. His wife (Kate Mulgrew) and his kids are leaving him, he has a new budding romance with a girl named Olivia (Olivia Brown), he doesn't know how to write his book, and his students of his creative writing class are stranger than him. However, one student (Danny DeVito) is extra strange. He lives with his crazy Momma (Anne Hathaway) and he can't get out of his relationship with her. And than he tries to kill hisma, making his life go from just crazy, to extra crazy! This movie is a work of art! The jokes, the characters, the whole script is near perfect. And Danny DeVito has proved to everyone he's more than a great actor, he's a great director. His kid's movie Matilda is among the best movies, and now he has one of the best comedies ever made. It's a black comedy, the jokes are about murder, but it's damn funny! And all the actors are at their full potential, whether they're main characters (Billy Crystal) or just one-bit minor characters (Olivia Brown). If you like comedy (who doesn't?), you'll love this movie. 10 stars.

It is hard to put the devastating beauty of Traffik to words, partly because I am still grasping to comprehend it myself, several hours after my second viewing. First, it must be said that Traffik contains some of the most incomparably and unforgettably haunting scenes I have seen in a film or television production. The acting is excellent, particularly that of Bill Paterson as a British minister grappling with his heroin-addicted daughter and an aid deal to Pakistan that hinges on drug issues. Another plot line describes these drug issues at a ground level in Pakistan, and revolves around a struggling opium poppy farmer and his interaction with a successful heroin smuggler. The third main storyline involves the prosecution of a Hamburg drug importer, and the conflicting efforts of his wife and two German detectives while he is under trial. It is a profound accomplishment that the interaction between these stories feels natural, transcending the forced plot entanglement often found in Hollywood movies. It is an even greater accomplishment that a work spread over three countries and half a dozen main characters can be so focused and enthralling, without having to oversimplify. It is devastating--bleak and brutal but never apathetic. In short, Traffik is a rare work of film that handles challenging subjects with unmatched compassion and clarity.

It is hard to put the sheer beauty of Traffik to words, partly because I am still grasping to do so myself, several days after my second viewing. First, it must be said that Traffik contains some of the most powerful, nuanced, and unforgettably haunting performances I have seen in a film or on television. The three main stories, particularly that of Bill Hdon, a British minister dealing with his heroin-addicted daughter and an aid deal to Pakistan, are gripping and complex. The second story describes the drug trade at a ground level in Pakistan through the eyes of a struggling, impoverished poppy farmer and his interaction with a successful heroin smuggler. The third main story involves the prosecution of a Hamburg drug lord, and the heroic efforts of his wife and two police detectives while he is under custody. It is a profound achievement that the interaction between these stories feels natural and seamless, without forced plot points or gaps in the narrative. It is an even greater achievement that a film spread over three hours and covering a lot of matter can be so focused and so clear, without attempting to oversimplify. It is funny--bleakly so--and deeply moving. In short, Traffik is a rare work of art that tackles challenging themes with unmatched skill and.

the first Child's Play was an original and effective little horror movie. as expected though, the 2 horrible sequels seemed to spell the end for this franchise. well, when i heard they were making a 4th one called "bride of chucky" i just rolled my eyes and muttered a "...when will they ever learn." but when i heard that they had gotten a great director, Ronny Yu and a solid cast including the awe inspiring Jennifer Tilly my interest in it perked up. this film is extremely well done. it has a great sense of humor, highly stylized graphic violence, great cinematography and the stunningly sexy Jennifer Tilly strutting her most impressive stuff during the first half. (i should add that she is also a fantastic actress as well.) it keeps it's tongue firmly in cheek without veering into campy territory. the doll effects are great and the verbal interplay between them is priceless. it's more of a horror/comedy than straight horror but the humor is welcome and well integrated. i've already heard that they're planning a Son of Chucky. if they can match the quality of this film, than maybe this franchise will have made a legitimate comeback. rating:8.5

the original Child's Play was an interesting and effective little horror movie. as usual though, the 2 horrible sequels seemed to spell the end for the franchise. well, when i heard they were making another movie, this one called "Dolls of the Dead" i just rolled my eyes. of course, this will be a disaster. but when i heard that they had gotten a great director in Ronny Yu and a solid cast including the awe inspiring Jennifer Tilly my interest was immediately perked up. the movie is very well done. it has a great mix of humor, a good amount of violence, great special effects and the stunningly beautiful Jennifer Tilly strutting her stuff in a very little doll outfit. (i must add that she is also a great actress as well) the movie keeps its tongue firmly in cheek without veering into gy territory. the doll effects are great and the banter between characters is great. it's more of a horror/comedy than straight horror but the horror is welcome and well integrated. i've also heard that they're planning a couple of sequels. if they can match the quality of this film, i think the franchise will survive for a long time. rating 8.5

Meanwhile, Tom is a modern man who does not believe in the social norms of the time. He speaks his mind and follows his heart. The movie stays true to the original novel by Mary Webb and is a delight from beginning to end.

In a way, the super being reminds me of one of Star Trek's most iconic episodes, Next Generation's "The Entity". This episode is also notable for creating a unique situation: this is the first time the cat is part of the action, and it allows the audience to see what an endearing character Uhuara can be when the situation allows her. Too bad no other episodes have explored this iconic character.

This 3 hour epic (seems much shorter) explores the will to power and conquest and the conflicting motives that underlie that quest by tracking two parallel lives: the emperor Q'in, whose desire to unify the Chinese feudal states has its basis in noble aims but devolves into violent oppression,isolation, and ultimate powerlessness; and the assassin Jing ke, a mercenary killer who comes to recognize the unintended consequences of murder and finds a form of salvation. As with all great art, this can be understood on many levels. The movie evoked for me images and ideas from Homer, Euripides, Machiavelli, Shakespeare, and Freud. The story itself is true (I checked it out at britannica.com!), so this film will appeal to history buffs. It's ironic that Q'in spent much of his last years in a futile quest for immortality (not shown on the screen, but consistent with the plot). The movie can also be viewed as an allegory of Maoism and the Cultural Revolution. Through the movie, one can understand that the last 50 years of Chinese history have had their precedent in the last 3000. Fortunately for the audience, these complex ideas are developed in a film that is rich in imagery, action, and pagent. The battle scenes alone are worth the price of admission.

This 3 hour epic (2005) explores the will to power and control and the complex motives that underlie that quest by tracking two main characters: the Emperor Q'in, whose quest to unify China's feudal states on the basis of philosophical aims quickly devolves into violent conquest, murder, and ultimate immortality; and the assassin Jing ke, a merciless killer who comes to understand the unintended consequences of murder and the true nature of power. The story is historically accurate (I checked it on the britannica website), so the film will appeal to history buffs. It's true that Q'in spent much of his later years on a failed quest for immortality (not shown in the film, but consistent with the plot). The film can also be viewed as an allegory of Maoism and the Cultural Revolution. Through the film, one can understand that the last 50 years of Chinese history are being played out in the last few minutes of the film. For the general audience, the philosophical ideas are developed in a story that is rich in action, drama, and pagent. It's well worth the price of admission

This was my late wife's favorite film. I'm sorry she did not live long enough to have the video as I'm sure she would have worn it out. What can we say? A great romantic story and the push off of two great men, the Raisuli and Teddy Rex. Sean Connery and Brian Keith are great in these roles. But while Connery is his usual sexy sex, it's the late Brian Keith who gives us a solid performance as the mercurial Teddy Roosevelt. Back up is provided with Candy Bergen, gorgeous in her early 30s, as the kidnapped American widow. Great back-up also comes from the great John Huston as Teddy's beleaguered SecState, John Hay; Geoffrey Lewis, from the Clint Eastwood films is great as the hesitant US Ambassador, Gummere; the late Vladek Sheybal with his demonically evil stare is great as the Beshaw and more is given by Steve Kanaly and Roy Jensen whose faces we have seen in several backgrounds. All in all, this is a film filled with wonderful romance, mindful of an era long gone. Mindless story? Not at all. The issue of big nations pushing around smaller ones for their own hegemonical interests is as true today as it was then. Overly romantic? Not really-- certainly not maudlin in any sense. Fun to watch? You bet. I own the video and will watch it again and again. I suggest you do the same.

Back up is provided with Candy Clark, gorgeous in her early days, as the beautiful First woman, Edith Roosevelt. Great back up also comes from the late John Huston, as the beleaguered SecState, John Hay. Geoffrey Lewis, from the Clint Eastwood films is great as the hesitant US Ambassador, Henry Kissot; and, Vladek Sheybal gives his usual menacing stare as the Tsar Tsar. Much more is given by Steve Kanaly and Roy Roberts, faces I have seen in several films. All in all, this is a film filled with great romance, mindful of an era long gone, and a story relevant to us all. The issue of big nations pushing around smaller nations for their own gain and gain, is just as true today as it was then. Overly sentimental? Not really, and not maudlin in any sense. Fun to watch? You bet. I own the video and will watch it again and again. I suggest you do the same.

An enjoyable 50's Western. I have it in my collection and recommend it to Western fans. It has a lot of action, and is quite well done in my estimation. The story is about a trapper wanted by a frontier post as a serial killer. He killed three of them on their land and took their possessions. They hire him to work at their post. Victor has a lot of trouble with the other employees, and lives off of the post without much regard to regulations. He is liked by the cook, but not the boss or much of the other employees. The story is good, not great, and it slides along to a satisfaction. Westerns of this kind are in a class of their own and perhaps never will be made much again. One to own. I give it a 7 rating. Maybe 6.8. I always find these films more enjoyable over time. For film noir fans..."The Big Steal" "They Live By Night" "Side Street" are most wonderful and to be enjoyed. Bought them all. Noir seems to parallel Westerns in a way. Some long, some never.

I hate to admit it, but I didn't find it to be one of Hitchcock's best but nonetheless a riveting, climatic thriller. In a remake of Hitchock's 1934 movie of the same title, Dr. Ben McKenna (James Stewart)  the man who knows too much - and his wife Jo McKenna (Doris Day) are holidaying in Morocco with their son Hank (Christopher Oslen) when there is a case of mistaken identity and caught up in the web of an assassination plot. The conspirators go to extreme lengths to prevent them from interfering with their plot: kidnapping their beloved Hank. I found it surprising that Doris Day, who I usually associate with Rock Hudson comedies, was cast in a Hitchcock film. As I was watching it, I soon realized that this was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other works (example: Psycho) and she had singing ability needed to pull off "Que Sera Sera", which she did beautifully. She was well cast as herself and James Stewart had chemistry, which helped make the couple believable. In comparison to the great director's other works I believe this isn't as good, but it is still a exceedingly entertaining family thriller/mystery. There is also the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day. Well directed, well acted. A fine film.

I hate to admit it, but I didn't find this to be one of Hitchcock's best films or a riveting thriller at all. In a remake of Hitchock's 1954 movie of the same name, Dr. Hank McKenna (James Stewart)  the man who knows too much, and his wife, Mara (Doris Day) are on vacation in Spain with their two children and their dog. However, there is a case of mistaken identity that traps them in the web of an international conspiracy. The leaders of Spain,, wanting to prevent anyone from interfering with their plans, decide to kill Hank. I found it surprising that Doris Day, who I usually associate with Rock Hudson's films, was cast in this spy thriller. As I started watching it, I soon realized that it was more of a family film than a spy thriller. The best part of the film was Doris Day's ability to successfully pull off "Que Sera Sera", which she did beautifully. Doris Day was cast as herself and James Stewart had to work hard to make his character believable. In comparison to some of Hitchcock's other works I believe this film is a disappointment, but it is still a exceedingly entertaining spy thriller to watch. There is also the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day. Well directed and well acted. A classic.

Martin Ritt's first film offers an exceptional existentialist answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised Kazan's offensive theme of trying to justify naming names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart Sidney Poitier daring to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although the quite appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and violence has hardly aged at all. One wonders how shocked initial 1957 moviegoers were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (if some of the bigoted didn't leave the theater early, they must of left dumbfounded, if not offended). The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewers will not realize what a radical and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: how it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school or college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever at all.

Well, this is a film that holds up well in comparison (many years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited greatly from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who could carry Kazan's conservative out of the theater and the courtroom (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart cast of unknowns actors willing to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to touch, such as workers' rights and civil rights. "Edge of the City" benefits greatly from this (then) unknown cast, and while the casting of black actors (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood dated, the courageous stand against thinly-disguised bigotry and violence has not aged at all. One scene even shocked initial audiences, as many white moviegoers were unprepared by a bold presentation of white supremacy. (If any of these bigoted individuals did leave the theater early, they must of been shocked and frightened, rather than offended.) The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to shy away from controversial issues, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most blind of viewers will not see what a powerful and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. Perhaps the most tragic of a lost opportunity: this film sadly remains unavailable in DVD format, for reasons that remain somewhat cloudy. This film should be required viewing in all history or social studies classes across the country, yet one can only see it on cable or satellite TV, if ever at all

Steamboat Willy was not the first cartoon to feature Mickey Mouse. The first film to star America's friend was "Plane Crazy". "Plane Crazy" was released May 15th 1928 in Hollywood California,in the silent movie format. "Steamboat Willy" was released November 18th 1928 as a SOUND movie (it was also released July 29th 1928 as a silent film). Thus making "Steamboat.."the first SOUND film of Mickey but NOT the first film for the little American Mouse. While many game shows have used the question: "What was the first appearance of Mickey Mouse?" The true answer is "Plane Crazy" not "Steamboat Willy". These dates can be checkout on IMDb under "release dates".

As always Joan Hickson is wonderful as Jane M. Subtle, sharp and aware. I do not wish to dwell on her acting skills as they are praised enough on this site. I would like to criticize some of the smaller parts as the rest of the cast seemed to be hand picked by director David Tucker. Liz Fraser's performance as Mrs. Bent (the mother of the missing girl Nora) is a joy to watch. Subtle and deeply moving as the alcohol-depending grieving mother who loves and misses her daughter desperately. A good long shot of her monologue (thanks Tucker!) so she can be enjoyed to the fullest. I was moved when I saw her the first time when it was broadcast and I am moved again, now I have it on DVD. Brava. Joanna Hole as Madge the tour-guide I find highly amusing. She is on the edge of over-acting but her role can have it. She is SO funny as the over-organized guide who wants to do good with everyone on that bus, I find her hilarious. Her reaction after she boarded every-one on the bus is great... As always: to perform comedy one has to take it very seriously, and that's what Ms Hole does. I do hope those two ladies have good careers (as I live in Holland I do not know if they have, not all theater productions can be googled...) -their performances on the screen deserve it. Pieter

I find Ms Hickson's performance as Jane the Girl to be very moving and powerful. I will not go into detail about her acting skills as they are praised enough on this site. I would like to praise some of the other actors in the cast of Jane who seem to be hand picked by Ms Hickson. Liz Fraser's performance as Mrs. Thompson (the mother of the missing girl Nora) is a short of brilliant. Subtle and nuanced portrayal as an alcohol-depending single mother who loves and misses her daughter desperately. In the long shot of her monologue (thanks Tucker Jones) she can be enjoyed to the fullest. I was moved when I saw it the first time when it was broadcast and I am moved again as now I have it on DVD. Wonderful performance. Joanna Greenwood as Betty, the bus-guide I find very funny. She is on the edge of over-acting but her performance does have it. She is SO funny as the over-organized woman who wants to do something with everyone on the bus and is very very it. Her reaction after she finds no-one on the bus is great... To pull off a dark comedy one has to do it very well, and that's what Ms Walters does. I do hope that those who have this DVD (as I live in Holland I do not have it and it is not a DVD that can be googled...) can update me on the availability of it. Pieter

The Three Stooges have always been some of the funniest actors that I have loved. I have just about every one of their shorts that they have made. I love all six of the stooges (Curly, Shemp, Moe, Larry, Joe, and Curly II)! All of their shorts are so funny and star many other great actors and actresses. A lot of effort was put into making the shorts! In my opinion the Three Stooges are some of the funniest actors ever and are the all time funniest comedy team! One of the most hilarious Three Stooges shorts is Men in Black. In this short are Bud Jamison, Bne Roberts, Phyllis Stanley, Dell Henderson, 'Big Billy' Rhodes, Billy Gilbert, and John Hiatt. All of these actors are great especially by Jamison and Henderson. There are many funny scenes here that I think most Three Stooges fans will love! In my opinion this one is the most different and funniest of ever. I highly recommend this one to all

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

I got Monster Man in a box set of three, where I disliked the other two but was in for a pleasant surprise with this. It mixes horror and comedy in reasonable amounts, helped out considerably by the solid performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Robert Urich as the monster villain, and Tanna.er as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but is fun to watch with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't live up to the classic gory comedies, but this is just fine. Director Michael Davis does have one or two great shots, such as in the bathroom gore scene, and the film is well-paced throughout if a bit predictable in twists and turns. For me it only falls off a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a character from Slipknot and the film tries to go body horror style but isn't twisted or clever enough. The final scene feels a bit contrived as well. Overall, if you like gore and horror comedies, this film is for you. It may not be a gnarly splatter comedy, but it's a fun ride all the same.
